speaker: Xingyan Chen, Cheuk Group
content: Title: Observation of van der Waals shielding between polar molecules in optical tweezersAbstract: Ultracold molecules typically suffer fast two-body loss at near-universal rates, and suppressing this loss has so far required strong DC or microwave electric fields. rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Title: Observation of van der Waals shielding between polar molecules in optical tweezers Abstract: Ultracold molecules typically suffer fast two-body loss at near-universal rates, and suppressing this loss has so far required strong DC or microwave electric fields. Recently, it has been predicted that particular pairs of molecular states can instead be shielded at zero field by repulsive van der Waals (vdW) interactions arising from either rotational or hyperfine structure. Here, we report the first experimental observation of both rotational and hyperfine vdW shielding, in collisions between pairs of laser-cooled CaF molecules trapped in optical tweezers. We observe inelastic loss suppressed by more than three orders of magnitude below the universal rate, and from measurements of thermalization we place a lower bound of 10³ on the elastic-to-inelastic ratio. We also observe three-body collisions in these shielded state combinations by deterministically preparing three molecules in a single tweezer and reading out the resulting state-resolved populations. Finally, I will present ongoing work of digital evaporative cooling of molecules. Lunch will be provided at 12:00 PM in EQuad J401.

speaker: Zohreh Davoudi, University of Maryland
content: Title: Quantum-computing frontiers in nuclear and particle physics Abstract: How does matter evolve in the early universe or in high-energy particle collisions? What does the phase diagram of strongly interacting matter look like? How does a large nucleus respond dynamically to probes of new physics? Large, reliable quantum computers hold the promise of addressing these questions through first-principles simulations of matter. In this talk, I will motivate a quantum-computing program in nuclear and particle physics and describe progress
rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Title: Quantum-computing frontiers in nuclear and particle physics Abstract: How does matter evolve in the early universe or in high-energy particle collisions? What does the phase diagram of strongly interacting matter look like? How does a large nucleus respond dynamically to probes of new physics? Large, reliable quantum computers hold the promise of addressing these questions through first-principles simulations of matter. In this talk, I will motivate a quantum-computing program in nuclear and particle physics and describe progress toward simulating systems governed by the fundamental interactions of the Standard Model or their effective descriptions. I will present current resource estimates for selected problems and showcase recent advances in implementations on quantum hardware and in theory-algorithm-experiment codesign. These advances are laying the groundwork for addressing fundamental questions in nuclear and particle physics with quantum computers. A light lunch will be served in the Bowen Atrium at 11:45am.

title: Static-Field Shielding of Bosonic Molecules: Evaporation to Degeneracy and Self
speaker: Bound Droplets - Laura Futamura, Bakr Group
content: Title: Static-Field Shielding of Bosonic Molecules: Evaporation to Degeneracy and Self-Bound DropletsAbstract: The strong, tunable dipolar interactions of ultracold molecules make them a powerful platform for quantum many-body physics, but reaching degeneracy by evaporative cooling requires suppressing inelastic collisions. Microwave collisional shielding has enabled the preparation of degenerate Fermi gases and Bose-Einstein condensates of polar molecules, whereas static electric field shielding has been limited to fermionic species, which are less
rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Title: Static-Field Shielding of Bosonic Molecules: Evaporation to Degeneracy and Self-Bound Droplets Abstract: The strong, tunable dipolar interactions of ultracold molecules make them a powerful platform for quantum many-body physics, but reaching degeneracy by evaporative cooling requires suppressing inelastic collisions. Microwave collisional shielding has enabled the preparation of degenerate Fermi gases and Bose-Einstein condensates of polar molecules, whereas static electric field shielding has been limited to fermionic species, which are less prone to inelastic loss. We demonstrate static-field Förster shielding of bosonic 23^Na87^Rb molecules, suppressing two-body loss by up to four orders of magnitude. Within a bound-state-free electric-field window, three-body loss is also strongly suppressed, enabling efficient evaporation. Evaporating with an efficiency of 2.09(9), we increase the phase-space density of the gas by two orders of magnitude, reaching degeneracy with 7200(1000) molecules. We observe self-bound droplets at the end of evaporation over a wide range of field strengths, emerging from either degenerate or non-degenerate parent gases. We perform Path Integral Monte Carlo simulations, which suggest that the observed droplets are filamentary in nature, and find good agreement with the experimentally observed droplet formation temperatures. Our results establish Förster shielding as a single-field route to prepare degenerate gases and self-bound droplets of bosonic polar molecules. Lunch will be provided at 12:00 PM in EQuad J401.

title: Quantum error correction with trapped ions
speaker: Andrew Potter, Quantinuum
content: Title: Quantum error correction with trapped ionsAbstract: To unlock the full power of quantum computers, fault-tolerant computation with error-corrected logical qubits must achieve the ultralow error rates needed for large-scale applications. This talk will highlight recent experimental progress in quantum error correction (QEC) and fault-tolerant logical operations on Quantinuum’s Helios, a 98-qubit trapped-ion quantum processor. First, I will describe demonstrations of exponential error suppression with increasing code distance for quantum
rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Title: Quantum error correction with trapped ions Abstract: To unlock the full power of quantum computers, fault-tolerant computation with error-corrected logical qubits must achieve the ultralow error rates needed for large-scale applications. This talk will highlight recent experimental progress in quantum error correction (QEC) and fault-tolerant logical operations on Quantinuum’s Helios, a 98-qubit trapped-ion quantum processor. First, I will describe demonstrations of exponential error suppression with increasing code distance for quantum memory and two-qubit logic using triangular color codes. These experiments achieved record-low logical failure rates around one error per 200,000 operations. Further, logical errors falling by more than an order of magnitude at each successive increase in code size. Second, I will present experimental validation of quantum memory and fast computation using the c4-helix code — a [[20,2,6]] non-planar code with encoding rate nearly 4x higher than surface codes, which supports a large set of fast logical Clifford gates through “instantaneous” virtual qubit relabeling (code automorphisms). A light lunch will be served in the Bowen Atrium at 11:45am.

title: Atomic Precision at Wafer Scale for Electronic and Quantum Technologies
speaker: Sheldon Zheng, MIT
content: Title: Atomic Precision at Wafer Scale for Electronic and Quantum TechnologiesAbstract: Progress in solid-state electronics has been driven by increasingly precise control over electrons, atoms, and interfaces. From controlled doping to high-κ/metal-gate stacks and gate-all-around nanosheets, each generation of silicon CMOS technology has depended on engineering matter at the scale of a few atoms. Superconducting quantum computing rests on a similar foundation: the nonlinearity that defines a qubit comes from a Josephson junction whose tunnel barrier
rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Title: Atomic Precision at Wafer Scale for Electronic and Quantum Technologies Abstract: Progress in solid-state electronics has been driven by increasingly precise control over electrons, atoms, and interfaces. From controlled doping to high-κ/metal-gate stacks and gate-all-around nanosheets, each generation of silicon CMOS technology has depended on engineering matter at the scale of a few atoms. Superconducting quantum computing rests on a similar foundation: the nonlinearity that defines a qubit comes from a Josephson junction whose tunnel barrier is an amorphous oxide about one nanometer thick. For future computing, from energy-efficient AI hardware to scalable quantum processors, a key challenge is to extend atomic-scale control to new materials and interfaces without sacrificing wafer-scale manufacturability. In this talk, I will introduce physical principles that allow atomic precision and wafer-scale manufacturing to coexist for emerging electronic and quantum technologies. First, I will present surface-kinetics-controlled synthesis of an air-stable monolayer superconductor at the inch scale, which reaches a kinetic inductance of ~0.7 nH/sq in superconducting circuits, together with atomically thin n-type and p-type semiconductors for CMOS applications. Second, I will discuss electrostatic-force-enabled transfer and heterogenous integration of these materials onto functional electronic and superconducting circuits with clean, minimally damaged interfaces. Finally, I will show how nano-scale strain modulates the band structures in ultra-scaled 2D transistors, delivering on-currents above 1 mA/µm at 1 V with CMOS-compatible contacts. These studies, spanning material synthesis, interface formation, and device engineering, demonstrate that atomic precision can be achieved at wafer scale and open new opportunities for energy-efficient electronics and scalable quantum technologies.

title: Photon-Mediated Interactions for Quantum Sensing and Simulation
speaker: James Thompson, University of Colorado, Boulder
content: Title: Photon-Mediated Interactions for Quantum Sensing and Simulation Abstract: Modern atomic physics enables remarkable control over the quantum states of atoms. This control underlies technologies such as precision timekeeping and navigation, and provides sensitive probes of new physics. An important frontier is to understand how to sculpt interactions between atoms so that they develop correlations and entanglement. Such collective quantum behavior can enhance the
rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Title: Photon-Mediated Interactions for Quantum Sensing and Simulation Abstract: Modern atomic physics enables remarkable control over the quantum states of atoms. This control underlies technologies such as precision timekeeping and navigation, and provides sensitive probes of new physics. An important frontier is to understand how to sculpt interactions between atoms so that they develop correlations and entanglement. Such collective quantum behavior can enhance the sensitivity of measurements and enable the simulation of other quantum systems. One promising approach uses photons trapped between highly reflecting mirrors. As photons bounce back and forth between the mirrors, they can mediate interactions between laser-cooled atoms held between the mirrors. In this talk, I will discuss our efforts to sculpt these photon-mediated interactions and expand the range of collective quantum phenomena that can be realized [1-7]. I will highlight how these engineered interactions can be used to simulate the dynamical phases of superconductors [8-11] and to improve the performance of matter-wave interferometers based on de Broglie waves [2-5, 12] and optical atomic clocks [13-15]. title: Strain Engineering of Nickelate Freestanding Membranes
speaker: Xin Wei, Stanford
content: Title: Strain Engineering of Nickelate Freestanding MembranesAbstract: Rare-earth nickelates host a rich landscape of electronic phases, including metal-to-insulator transitions and superconductivity, reflecting the interplay between strong electronic correlations and lattice degrees of freedom. Strain offers a powerful means of tuning these phases, but conventional epitaxial thin films are constrained by a limited and discrete strain range and device-to-device variability. Freestanding membranes overcome these limitations, opening new opportunities
rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Title: Strain Engineering of Nickelate Freestanding Membranes Abstract: Rare-earth nickelates host a rich landscape of electronic phases, including metal-to-insulator transitions and superconductivity, reflecting the interplay between strong electronic correlations and lattice degrees of freedom. Strain offers a powerful means of tuning these phases, but conventional epitaxial thin films are constrained by a limited and discrete strain range and device-to-device variability. Freestanding membranes overcome these limitations, opening new opportunities to explore and control correlated quantum states. Building on recent advances in sacrificial-layer synthesis of oxide freestanding membranes1 and their demonstrated stability under extreme strain, we developed a cryogenic in situ stage for tensile-strain manipulation2 and a high-pressure platform with quasi-2D membrane and electrical-contact fabrication inside a diamond anvil cell3. In this talk, I will present how these capabilities enable systematic investigations of strain-tunable electronic and magnetic phase transitions in NdNiO3 membranes4. I will then discuss the relationship between superconducting transition temperature (Tc) and superfluid density in Nd1-xSrxNiO2 membranes under tensile strain5, followed by the pronounced enhancement of superconductivity under high pressure, with Tc observed near liquid-nitrogen temperature3. Together, these studies established strain-engineering of freestanding membranes as a reliable platform for investigating coupling among lattice, electronic and magnetic degrees of freedom and expand the accessible parameter space for engineering quantum phases. 1. title: New Frontiers in Quantum Simulation of Strongly Correlated Matter with Ultracold Atoms
speaker: Anant Kale, Harvard
content: Title: New Frontiers in Quantum Simulation of Strongly Correlated Matter with Ultracold AtomsAbstract: Quantum simulation of strongly correlated matter is a promising probe of fundamental physics while also being practically useful in making progress on long-standing problems in condensed matter. A paradigmatic example is understanding the physics of high-Tc cuprate materials, where many open questions remain regarding the origin and nature of unconventional superconductivity, pseudogap phase, and spin and charge stripes. Ultracold fermionic atoms in
rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Title: New Frontiers in Quantum Simulation of Strongly Correlated Matter with Ultracold Atoms Abstract: Quantum simulation of strongly correlated matter is a promising probe of fundamental physics while also being practically useful in making progress on long-standing problems in condensed matter. A paradigmatic example is understanding the physics of high-Tc cuprate materials, where many open questions remain regarding the origin and nature of unconventional superconductivity, pseudogap phase, and spin and charge stripes. Ultracold fermionic atoms in optical lattices provide a clean and controllable realization of the Fermi-Hubbard model, believed to capture the essential physics of the cuprates. In this talk, I will describe our recent experimental results achieving a several-fold reduction in temperature, reaching a regime inaccessible to numerical simulation. Using equilibrium and dynamical probes, we experimentally characterize the pseudogap phase, thought to be a parent state for the d-wave superconductor. In the pseudogap regime, we observe novel peaks versus doping in the compressibility and nematic susceptibility, possible precursors to charge and spin stripes. We also observe direct signatures of spin stripes at the lowest temperatures, although these appear to differ from the conventional picture of stripes. Finally, I will describe ongoing efforts to push beyond the plain Hubbard model, including a three-band Lieb lattice and next-nearest-neighbor hopping t′, which may play an important role in understanding the long-sought-after high-Tc superconductivity.

I will highlight some of the strongest known results, including my work introducing the magic hierarchy, a framework that
rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Title: Why is it so hard to prove the limits of quantum circuits? Abstract: Although almost all quantum states require exponentially large quantum circuits to prepare, it remains a central challenge to prove that even very restricted circuits cannot prepare specific states. In this talk, I will describe the landscape of what we can currently prove about the limits of quantum circuits, known as circuit lower bounds. I will highlight some of the strongest known results, including my work introducing the magic hierarchy, a framework that unifies several circuit models, including those with intermediate measurements. I will also discuss my work on a quantum analogue of the natural proofs barrier, which identifies obstacles to extending existing lower-bound techniques to more powerful circuits.

speaker: Joern Bannies, UC Berkeley
content: Title: Controlling the nodal-loop topology of LaSbxTe2-xAbstract: In crystalline materials, the crystal symmetry can impose strong constraints on the electronic structure. Highly symmetric square-nets, for example, guarantee the existence of several line-node degeneracies in the electronic structure of square-net materials. rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Title: Controlling the nodal-loop topology of LaSbxTe2-x Abstract: In crystalline materials, the crystal symmetry can impose strong constraints on the electronic structure. Highly symmetric square-nets, for example, guarantee the existence of several line-node degeneracies in the electronic structure of square-net materials. However, manipulating the underlying crystalline symmetries to achieve experimental control over topological states remains challenging. In this talk, I will establish a symmetry-based framework that describes the electronic structure evolution of square-net materials upon breaking fourfold and n glide symmetry and demonstrate its application to the LaSbxTe2-x system. Using angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES), I will show that breaking n glide symmetry opens a gap of several hundred meV in the Dirac nodal loop, gapping out almost the entire Fermi surface. The main control parameter for this topological phase transition is electron doping, as achieved by bulk chemical substitution or reversible in situ surface potassium deposition. On the local atomic scale, however, the phase transition can be realized even without the need of doping. Scanning tunneling microscopy and spectroscopy (STM/S) show strong signatures of gap closing on naturally existing twin domain walls of the gapped nodal-loop phase, where the n glide symmetry is locally restored compared to the bulk. This work places LaSbxTe2-x as a unique and highly tunable system, where the nodal-loop topology can be controlled not only by doping but also local structural modulations.

rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Title: Quantum Precision Measurement for Fundamental Physics Abstract: We will present a new experiment to measure CP violation beyond the Standard Model using ²²⁹ThF⁺ molecular ions. The ²²⁹Th nucleus has an enhanced Schiff moment due to its octupole deformation and can be efficiently produced using nuclear clock technologies. title: Many-body effects in high harmonic generation from quantum matter
speaker: Mingyao Guo, Caltech
content: Title: Many-body effects in high harmonic generation from quantum matter Abstract: Quantum materials host intertwined charge, spin, orbital, and lattice degrees of freedom, providing a rich setting for exploring light–matter interactions. In the strong-field regime, high harmonic generation (HHG) connects coherent electron dynamics driven by intense lightwaves to extremely nonlinear light emission. Yet how many-body interactions shape this process on sub-optical-cycle timescales remains an open question. In this talk, I will highlight our
rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Title: Many-body effects in high harmonic generation from quantum matter Abstract: Quantum materials host intertwined charge, spin, orbital, and lattice degrees of freedom, providing a rich setting for exploring light–matter interactions. In the strong-field regime, high harmonic generation (HHG) connects coherent electron dynamics driven by intense lightwaves to extremely nonlinear light emission. Yet how many-body interactions shape this process on sub-optical-cycle timescales remains an open question. In this talk, I will highlight our recent efforts to understand and control HHG in quantum matter. I will first demonstrate how collective magnetism emerging at millielectronvolt energies enables switching of HHG on the petahertz frequency scale in an antiferromagnet. Turning from manipulation of the harmonic yield to the structure of the emission spectrum, I will then present our discovery of non-integer HHG arising from strong electron correlations in a cuprate Mott insulator. Together, these examples illustrate how high harmonic radiation can both reveal and be tailored by emergent many-body phenomena, opening new pathways towards lightwave electronics and attosecond technologies enabled by quantum materials.

title: Efficient photon and phonon interfaces for spin qubits in diamond
speaker: Marko Loncar, Harvard University
content: Title: Efficient photon and phonon interfaces for spin qubits in diamond Abstract: Color centers in diamond provide optically accessible, long-lived spin qubits that are promising building blocks for distributed quantum networks. Realizing scalable quantum nodes, however, requires efficient and controllable interfaces between spins and both photons and phonons. In this talk, I will describe our efforts to engineer the electromagnetic and elastic environments of silicon-vacancy (SiV) centers to realize efficient spin–photon and spin–phonon
rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Title: Efficient photon and phonon interfaces for spin qubits in diamond Abstract: Color centers in diamond provide optically accessible, long-lived spin qubits that are promising building blocks for distributed quantum networks. Realizing scalable quantum nodes, however, requires efficient and controllable interfaces between spins and both photons and phonons. In this talk, I will describe our efforts to engineer the electromagnetic and elastic environments of silicon-vacancy (SiV) centers to realize efficient spin–photon and spin–phonon interfaces. The SiV center exhibits large strain susceptibility, enabling coherent control of its orbital and spin degrees of freedom via mechanical excitations. Our early work demonstrated strain-based control of SiV coherence [1] and coherent acoustic driving of a single SiV spin [2], establishing the foundations of quantum phononics in diamond. Building on this, we recently demonstrated the acoustic Purcell effect in nanomechanical resonators coupled to color centers [3], as well as the formation of phonon-dressed spin states and engineered spin–phonon interactions in the strong-driving regime [4]. We further engineer the phononic local density of states using diamond phononic crystals with complete bandgaps centered around ~60 GHz [5]. By embedding single SiV centers within these structures, we observe up to an 18-fold suppression of single-phonon-induced orbital relaxation, which may extend spin coherence and enable control of phonon-mediated processes at elevated temperatures. Finally, we use strain to engineer diamond nanomechanical resonators themselves resulting in ultrahigh mechanical coherence (Q ≳ 10⁸), revealing microscopic two-level-system defects and establishing a materials foundation for ultra-low-loss phononic quantum interfaces [6]. Complementarily, nanofabricated photonic cavities coupled to diamond color centers have enabled high-efficiency spin–photon interfaces that form the backbone of quantum networking experiments. Such cavity-enhanced nodes were used to demonstrate memory-enhanced quantum communication over metropolitan-scale distances [7] and deterministic entanglement of nanophotonic quantum memory nodes in a telecommunication network [8]. Fabrication advances have recently allowed realization of high-Q photonic crystal cavities (Q ~ 1.8 × 10⁵ in the visible) [9] and slow-light photonic crystal waveguides [10], both fabricated in thin-film diamond. Together, these results establish a unified diamond platform in which both photon and phonon interfaces can be engineered with high precision. Such simultaneous control of electromagnetic and elastic degrees of freedom opens new opportunities for multiplexed quantum repeaters, quantum acoustodynamics, and hybrid quantum interconnects based on color centers in diamond.
